<h1>Research</h1>
<p>I study how water, plants, and chemistry interact in rivers and wetlands. My research ranges from the shape of the ground in a wetland to carbon cycling across river networks.</p>
<p>Below are my journal publications, grouped by subject, with a short explanation of each paper.</p>

<section class="research-section" aria-labelledby="anchorriveco">
<h2 id="anchorriveco">River carbon and metabolism</h2>
<p>How much carbon do rivers process themselves, and how much arrives from the surrounding landscape? My work on the Loire and on oxygen–carbon models separates these contributions. Changes in algae and aquatic plants matter, but flow, groundwater, and carbonate chemistry can change the carbon budget just as much.</p>
<ul class="papers">
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2024jg008401">A Coupled O2‐CO2 Model for Joint Estimation of Stream Metabolism, O‐C Stoichiometry, and Inorganic Carbon Fluxes</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Diamond, J. S.; Bertuzzo, E. (2025). <i>Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences 130, e2024JG008401</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">A model combining oxygen, inorganic carbon, and alkalinity to estimate metabolism and carbon fluxes together. It allows oxygen–carbon ratios to vary instead of assuming a fixed conversion.</p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/lno.70016">Inorganic carbon dynamics and their relation to autotrophic community regime shift over three decades in a large, alkaline river</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Diamond, J. S.; Truong, A. N.; Abril, G.; Bertuzzo, E.; Chanudet, V.; Lamouroux, R.; Moatar, F. (2025). <i>Limnology and Oceanography 70, 1122-1136</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Three decades of Loire River data show how discharge, carbonate chemistry, and changes in the autotrophic community affect inorganic carbon. Oxygen-based metabolism alone does not describe the full carbon budget.</p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-22-4923-2025">Multidecadal trends in CO₂ evasion and aquatic metabolism in a large temperate river</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Nguyen, A. T.; Abril, G.; Diamond, J. S.; Lamouroux, R.; Martinet, C.; Moatar, F. (2025). <i>Biogeosciences 22, 4923-4951</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">A 32-year record links declining Loire CO₂ emissions to changes in groundwater contributions. Catchment inputs help explain the long-term trend alongside changes in river metabolism.</p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/lno.11789">Metabolic regime shifts and ecosystem state changes are decoupled in a large river</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Diamond, J. S.; Moatar, F.; Cohen, M. J.; Poirel, A.; Martinet, C.; Maire, A.; Pinay, G. (2022). <i>Limnology and Oceanography 67, S54–S70</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">The Loire’s shift from phytoplankton to macrophytes did not produce an equally abrupt change in metabolism. Production and respiration changed on different timescales from the visible ecological state.</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="docs/Diamond%20et%20al_2021_RegimeShiftsLoire.pdf">PDF</a></p>
</li>
</ul></section>

<section class="research-section" aria-labelledby="headwater-stream-biogeochemistry">
<span id="anchorbgc"></span><h2 id="headwater-stream-biogeochemistry">Water quality and river networks</h2>
<p>Dissolved oxygen connects ecosystem processes to water quality. Across this work, a recurring finding is that timing and location matter: drying, storms, light, and wastewater inputs can produce very different conditions within the same river network. Long records and measurements across multiple sites help capture what occasional sampling misses.</p>
<ul class="papers">
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-17-3411-2025">OLIGOTREND, a global database of multi-decadal chlorophyll a and water quality time series for rivers, lakes, and estuaries</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Minaudo, C.; Abonyi, A.; Alcaraz, C.; Diamond, J.; Howden, N. J. K.; Rode, M.; Romero, E.; Thieu, V.; Worrall, F.; Zhang, Q.; Benito, X. (2025). <i>Earth System Science Data 17, 3411-3430</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">OLIGOTREND brings together 4.3 million observations from 1,894 locations to study long-term changes in chlorophyll and water quality. Declining nutrients do not always lead to matching declines in algae.</p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2024jg008369">Alternating Drying and Flowing Phases Control Stream Metabolism Through Short‐ and Long‐Term Effects: Insights From a River Network</a></h3>
<p class="citation">López‐Rojo, N.; Sarremejane, R.; Foulquier, A.; Singer, G.; Diamond, J.; Rioux, D.; Miquel, C.; Mulero, S.; Lionnet, C.; Peñas, F. J.; Rodeles, A. A.; Datry, T. (2025). <i>Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences 130, e2024JG008369</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Measurements across 20 reaches show how drying and rewetting affect stream production and respiration. The effects depend on both recent conditions and the duration of earlier dry periods.</p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolind.2023.109987">Hypoxia is common in temperate headwaters and driven by hydrological extremes</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Diamond, J. S.; Moatar, F.; Recoura-Massaquant, R.; Chaumot, A.; Zarnetske, J.; Valette, L.; Pinay, G. (2023). <i>Ecological Indicators 147, 109987</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Low oxygen occurred at 51 of 78 headwater sites. Drying, rewetting, and storms were major drivers, with warm, low-gradient streams particularly vulnerable.</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="docs/Diamond%20et%20al_2023_hypoxia.pdf">PDF</a></p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/lno.12271">Light and hydrologic connectivity drive dissolved oxygen synchrony in stream networks</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Diamond, J. S.; Pinay, G.; Bernal, S.; Cohen, M. J.; Lewis, D.; Lupon, A.; Zarnetske, J.; Moatar, F. (2023). <i>Limnology and Oceanography 68, 322-335</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Across five catchments, shared light conditions and hydrologic connectivity explained much of the synchrony in dissolved oxygen. This helps identify when one site can represent conditions elsewhere in a network.</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="docs/Diamond%20et%20al_2022_DOSynchrony.pdf">PDF</a></p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolind.2021.108233">Stream network variation in dissolved oxygen: Metabolism proxies and biogeochemical controls</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Diamond, J. S.; Bernal, S.; Boukra, A.; Cohen, M. J.; Lewis, D.; Masson, M.; Moatar, F.; Pinay, G. (2021). <i>Ecological Indicators 131, 108233</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Production increased predictably with stream size, while respiration varied more widely. Dissolved oxygen measurements also provided information about organic matter quality and denitrification potential.</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="docs/Diamond_ecoindicators.pdf">PDF</a></p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0256292">Large spatiotemporal variability in metabolic regimes for an urban stream draining four wastewater treatment plants with implications for dissolved oxygen monitoring</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Ledford, S. H.; Diamond, J. S.; Toran, L. (2021). <i>PLOS ONE 16, e0256292</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">A year of measurements around four wastewater treatment plants revealed strong seasonal and local differences in metabolism. Monitoring location and timing can substantially change the apparent effect of an outfall.</p>
</li>
</ul></section>

<section class="research-section" aria-labelledby="stream-temperature">
<h2 id="stream-temperature">Stream temperature</h2>
<p>Air temperature alone is a poor guide to the temperatures that river organisms experience. These studies examine how flow, groundwater, shade, dams, and ponds shape thermal conditions, from individual impoundments to regional and national river networks.</p>
<ul class="papers">
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-26-2583-2022">Regional, multi-decadal analysis on the Loire River basin reveals that stream temperature increases faster than air temperature</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Seyedhashemi, H.; Vidal, J. P.; Diamond, J. S.; Thiéry, D.; Monteil, C.; Hendrickx, F.; Maire, A.; Moatar, F. (2022). <i>Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 26, 2583-2603</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">A reconstruction of Loire basin temperatures from 1963–2019 found that many streams warmed faster than the air. Declining flows contributed to warming, while riparian shade moderated it in small streams.</p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-26-3477-2022">Spatial extrapolation of stream thermal peaks using heterogeneous time series at a national scale</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Beaufort, A.; Diamond, J. S.; Sauquet, E.; Moatar, F. (2022). <i>Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 26, 3477-3495</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Records from about 1,700 stations were used to estimate summer temperature peaks across France. The approach combines uneven monitoring records with information about local stream conditions.</p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.142667">Thermal signatures identify the influence of dams and ponds on stream temperature at the regional scale</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Seyedhashemi, H.; Moatar, F.; Vidal, J. P.; Diamond, J. S.; Beaufort, A.; Chandesris, A.; Valette, L. (2021). <i>Science of The Total Environment 766, 142667</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Five indicators derived from stream and air temperatures distinguished dam, pond, and relatively natural thermal regimes across 330 monitoring stations in the Loire basin.</p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-23-4509-2019">Small dams alter thermal regimes of downstream water</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Chandesris, A.; Van Looy, K.; Diamond, J. S.; Souchon, Y. (2019). <i>Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 23, 4509-4525</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Monitoring downstream of 11 small dams showed different effects on minimum and maximum temperatures. Impoundment area and water residence time helped explain those differences.</p>
</li>
</ul></section>

<section class="research-section" aria-labelledby="anchormicro">
<span id="wetland-biogeochemistry"></span><span id="plant-water-interactions-and-disturbance"></span><span id="ecohydrology"></span><h2 id="anchormicro">Wetland ecology and microtopography</h2>
<p>Small differences in ground elevation can organize an entire wetland. My work in black ash wetlands connects hummocks and hollows to vegetation, soil chemistry, and water levels, and asks how these relationships change when trees are lost to emerald ash borer.</p>
<ul class="papers">
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/wat2.1493">A little relief: Ecological functions and autogenesis of wetland microtopography</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Diamond, J. S.; Epstein, J. M.; Cohen, M. J.; McLaughlin, D. L.; Hsueh, Y.; Keim, R. F.; Duberstein, J. A. (2021). <i>WIREs Water 8, e1493</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">A synthesis of how wetland microtopography forms and persists, and why it matters for water storage, carbon cycling, and biodiversity. It connects plant–soil–water feedbacks with the development of hummocks and hollows.</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="docs/Diamond%20et%20al_2020_A%20little%20relief.pdf">PDF</a></p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.14014">Hydrologic variability in black ash wetlands: Implications for vulnerability to emerald ash borer</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Cianciolo, T. R.; Diamond, J. S.; McLaughlin, D. L.; Slesak, R. A.; D&#x27;Amato, A. W.; Palik, B. J. (2021). <i>Hydrological Processes 35, e14014</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Water-level records from 15 black ash wetlands show why vulnerability to tree loss differs among sites. Existing wetness and the vegetation that replaces ash help determine the hydrologic response.</p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-17-901-2020">Microtopography is a fundamental organizing structure of vegetation and soil chemistry in black ash wetlands</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Diamond, J. S.; McLaughlin, D. L.; Slesak, R. A.; Stovall, A. (2020). <i>Biogeosciences 17, 901-915</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Fine-resolution elevation measurements link hummocks to differences in vegetation and soil chemistry across ten wetlands. The ecological contrasts between hummocks and hollows were stronger at wetter sites.</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="docs/Diamond%20et%20al_2020_Microtopo%20organizing.pdf">PDF</a></p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2019.111271">Quantifying wetland microtopography with terrestrial laser scanning</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Stovall, A. E.; Diamond, J. S.; Slesak, R. A.; McLaughlin, D. L.; Shugart, H. (2019). <i>Remote Sensing of Environment 232, 111271</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Develops a terrestrial laser scanning approach for measuring wetland microtopography, making it possible to study small elevation differences across whole plots.</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="docs/Stovall%20et%20al_2019_TLS.pdf">PDF</a></p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-23-5069-2019">Pattern and structure of microtopography implies autogenic origins in forested wetlands</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Diamond, J. S.; McLaughlin, D. L.; Slesak, R. A.; Stovall, A. (2019). <i>Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 23, 5069-5088</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Hummock heights and spatial patterns across ten black ash wetlands support the idea that vegetation helps create its own elevated growing sites through feedbacks with water and soil.</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="docs/Diamond%20et%20al_Microtopo%20pattern.pdf">PDF</a></p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2018.05.082">Forested versus herbaceous wetlands: Can management mitigate ecohydrologic regime shifts from invasive emerald ash borer?</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Diamond, J. S.; McLaughlin, D. L.; Slesak, R. A.; D&#x27;Amato, A. W.; Palik, B. J. (2018). <i>Journal of Environmental Management 222, 436-446</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Examines the ecohydrologic consequences of black ash loss and possible management responses. Differences in water use between forested and herbaceous wetlands help explain the persistence of wetter conditions after tree loss.</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="docs/Diamond%20et%20al.%20%282018%29.pdf">PDF</a></p>
</li>
</ul></section>

<section class="research-section" aria-labelledby="watershed-hydrochemistry">
<span id="wetlandscape-connectivity"></span><span id="hydrology"></span><h2 id="watershed-hydrochemistry">Watershed hydrology</h2>
<p>Water movement determines when wetlands connect and which solutes reach rivers. These studies use water levels and concentration–discharge relationships to identify changes in flow paths that are difficult to see from occasional measurements.</p>
<ul class="papers">
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2018wr024652">Wetland Connectivity Thresholds and Flow Dynamics From Stage Measurements</a></h3>
<p class="citation">McLaughlin, D. L.; Diamond, J. S.; Quintero, C.; Heffernan, J.; Cohen, M. J. (2019). <i>Water Resources Research 55, 6018-6032</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">A water-budget method uses water-level records to estimate wetland connectivity thresholds and flows. In five Big Cypress wetlands, much of the export occurred during surface-water connections.</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="docs/McLaughlin%20et%20al_2019_Wetland%20connectivity.pdf">PDF</a></p>
</li>
<li class="paper"><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.11424">Complex patterns of catchment solute–discharge relationships for coastal plain rivers</a></h3>
<p class="citation">Diamond, J. S.; Cohen, M. J. (2018). <i>Hydrological Processes 32, 388-401</i>.</p>
<p class="paper-summary">Across 44 Florida rivers, solute concentrations often changed their relationship with discharge near median flow. A single power-law relationship can miss these shifts and bias estimates of solute export.</p>
<p class="paper-links"><a href="docs/Diamond%20and%20Cohen_2018.pdf">PDF</a></p>
</li>
</ul></section>
